One Chat Studio
MADE WITH CLAUDE · LAB EDU · 00:00:40:23

One chat.Fourteen roles.

A 41-second reel about how we make branded reels: our whole video team fits in one chat with Claude. Fourteen roles show up as slash cards, the editor proves it by cutting a raw 37-second take down to 24, and four more roles follow: subtitles, text behind you, the best take and any background. Everything on screen is drawn in code on an HTML canvas, timed to the voice word by word. This is the full workflow.

01 · The idea

A team, not a tool.

Most "made with AI" reels show a prompt and a result. This one shows the people you would normally hire for a branded reel, as roles that all live in one chat with Claude: the editor, subtitles, text behind the speaker, take selection, backgrounds, the hook, the voice, animation, lettering, 3D, sound, music, references and review.

The structure follows that idea. The hook types a request into a chat and the reply is a deck of role cards. One role gets a deep demo so the claim feels real (the editor cutting 37 seconds of raw talk to 24), four more get a quick demo each (/subtitles, /text-behind, /takes, /background), and the offer block shows what we do with your brand. Catalina, the Lab's character, presents it from the corner.

/hook/voice/cut/takes/subtitles/background/text-behind/animation/lettering/3d/sound/music/reference/review
02 · References

What Claude needed before the first prompt.

This is the Lab's own piece, so the brand is ours. We studied a reel we liked for its rhythm and its card language, frame by frame, and rebuilt the look from scratch. These are the ideas it leans on, in general terms.

Slash-command cards

Each role is a card named like a chat command (/cut, /takes). It reads as "you type it, it happens", which is exactly the promise of a team inside a chat.

Thick outlines, hard shadows

Cards with a thick black outline and a solid offset shadow, no blur. The look is graphic and loud, survives Instagram compression and stays readable on a phone.

A colour per block

Every block floods the whole frame with a new colour, alternating light and dark: clay, navy, cream, deep green, black, amber, navy, cream. The viewer feels each new role before reading it.

Props that break out

On stressed words, things leave their card: the caption jumps out of the /subtitles video as a sticker, the /text-behind shot explodes into its layers, rejected takes fall out, old sets fly off as polaroids.

Palette

The Lab's colours carry the frame; the role scenes add a few loud accents so each card reads at a glance.

#F6F0E6 cream#D97757 clay#141A2E navy
Presenter

Catalina, the Lab's character, from her real images: two short image-to-video clips for the opening and the close, and full-body poses from her character sheet in between, swapped in place.

03 · One-time setup

Before the prompt.

Step 01

Install Claude Code.

Follow the official guide at docs.claude.com (Claude Code overview) for your system, then open it inside an empty project folder.

Step 02

Node 22+ and FFmpeg.

The scenes are plain JavaScript drawing on an HTML canvas. Node runs a headless browser that renders each frame, and FFmpeg joins the frames and the audio into the MP4.

Step 03

Python 3.10+.

For the audio side: checking loudness, mixing the voice with the sound effects and reading the narration back with Whisper to confirm every word.

Step 04

An ElevenLabs API key.

Put it in a .env file in the project and ask Claude to request word-level timestamps with the audio. Those timestamps are what every cue reads.

Optional

A style guide for Claude.

A short Markdown file with your palette, fonts, pacing and safe zone, which Claude reads before writing any scene. We used a paid motion-design guide; your own notes work too.

04 · Claude session

One brief, then the checks.

Below is the master prompt you can paste, followed by the two quality-control messages: the stills review and the final render.

00:01 · master prompt · claude code
Make a 41-second vertical reel for The AI Editing Lab, 1080x1920 at 30 fps, all in English. It promotes our service: we make branded reels with Claude. The idea: our whole video team fits in one chat.

1. Script. Hook in under 2 seconds: "This is our whole video team, and it fits in one chat with Claude." Then 14 roles, and not one of them sits at an editing desk. Demo the editor in depth, then four more roles in one line each, roles no earlier reel of ours has shown: subtitles that land word by word, a title that slides behind the speaker, the best of three takes, and a background that becomes anywhere the brand needs. Then the offer: send us your brand and a reel you love, we match its rhythm, its colors and its style, with your voice. Close with: "Comment STUDIO and we'll make one for your brand."

2. Voice. ElevenLabs, voice "Jessica", natural speed (1.0). Save the start and end time of every word to words.json; every cue reads its time from a word, never from a guessed second.

3. Metaphor. A chat with Claude whose reply is a deck of 14 slash-command role cards: /hook /voice /cut /takes /subtitles /background /text-behind /animation /lettering /3d /sound /music /reference /review. Each demoed role gets one big card with its job happening inside, on a drawn talking-head video where it needs one. Make /cut the deep demo: a raw 37-second clip as word blocks over a waveform; pauses, mistakes and breaths get marked and snipped until it closes to 24 seconds.

4. Look. Everything drawn in code on an HTML canvas. One shared component kit: cards with thick black outlines and a hard offset shadow (no blur), clay #D97757 headers, a segmented progress bar on top. Every block gets its own full-frame background colour, alternating light and dark; the brand block is navy #141A2E and the close returns to cream #F6F0E6. On stressed words, props break out of their cards.

5. Layout. Every text and prop inside x 90-960 and y 250-1480, each block full at its cut. Keep the bottom-right corner empty for our presenter.

6. Build. Two builders in parallel sharing the kit: one does the frame, hook, team, brand and CTA; the other does the role scenes (/cut, /subtitles, /text-behind, /takes, /background). Sound effects only on real events, voice on top, mix to -14 LUFS, true peak at or below -1.5 dB.

7. Process. Show me a stills sheet and a motion and originality check before the final render, and wait for my approval.

What came back: the script, a block-by-block storyboard with every stressed word mapped to a change on screen, the ElevenLabs narration with 119 time-stamped words, a shared component kit, and two builders working in parallel: one on the frame, hook, team, brand and CTA, the other on the role scenes, all reading the same word clock.

00:02 · stills before render · claude code
Before the final render, export a stills sheet: one frame every 1.5 seconds from frame 0, with a red outline for the safe zone (x 90-960, y 250-1480). Check every block for: motion density (something changes at least once a second and on every stressed word), fill (is the block full at its cut, or does it start near-empty?), card size (does the card fill the hero zone, readable on a phone?), colour timing (does each background change land on the cut, not one block late?) and originality (is every prop drawn for this line, or is anything a generic placeholder? Does any block repeat a role, prop or structure from our earlier reels?). List everything you find, fix it all in one pass and show me the sheet again.

What came back: the first pass was mostly cream and read static; some blocks opened near-empty and the cards were small. The fix, in one pass: a full-frame colour per block, every block full at its cut, cards that fill the hero zone, and the flood moved to start just before each cut.

00:03 · final render · claude code
Approved. Now composite our presenter Catalina on top from her real images: her two short image-to-video clips at the start and at the end, and full-body poses from her character sheet in between, each swapped in place with a short crossfade on a block change; she never slides in or out. Render 1080x1920 at 30 fps, H.264 at 14 Mbps CBR, the mix at -14 LUFS, and give me a stills strip of the final.

What came back: 40.8 seconds at 1080×1920 and 30 fps, H.264 at 14 Mbps, the voice mixed to −14 LUFS.

05 · What Claude built

Fourteen roles, one kit.

/CUT · THE DEEP DEMO

37 seconds become 24

A raw clip of word blocks over a waveform, a ruler from 0 to 37 s. Each pause, mistake and breath is marked on the word that names it, giant scissors pass over them, the gaps close and the counter rolls to 24 and turns green, with a −13 s pill.

/SUBTITLES

Word by word

A talking-head video whose captions pop on each word's real start time, a live subtitles.srt log that writes one line per word, and loose word blocks that snap onto the waveform on "exactly". On "speak" the caption jumps out of the video as a sticker.

/TEXT-BEHIND

Behind you

A huge YOUR TITLE pops in front of a street shot, slides to the centre and drops behind the person on "behind". On "part" the shot explodes into three labelled layers (background, title, you) past the card's edges, then snaps back.

/TAKES

The best one stays

A pile of three takes fans out into a row, each a mini video with its waveform. Takes 1 and 2 show their stumble and get a red X; take 3 gets a BEST stamp, the rejects fall out of the card, and the winner slams into the timeline slot.

/BACKGROUND

Anywhere

The presenter as a cutout over a set that swaps on every stressed word (office, beach, street, neon city, a clay brand studio). Each old set flies out of the card as a polaroid, and the YOUR LOGO sign jumps over the corner.

BRAND

Your brand, a reel you love

A logo card and a reference reel feed an empty slot; the new reel takes the reference's cut rhythm, colours and caption style, then a waveform joins for your voice.

key code · common_studio.js · a colour per block
// every block floods its own full-frame colour, alternating light / dark
const ST_BLOCKS = [
  { t: 0, col: null, dark: false, em: null },                            // hook: cream paper
  { t: CUT_TEAM, col: ST_CLAY, dark: false, em: '#FFFFFF', x: 540, y: 900 },
  { t: CUT_CUT, col: ST_NAVY, dark: true, em: '#F08A64', x: 540, y: 750 },
  { t: CUT_SCRIPT, col: null, dark: false, em: null, x: 540, y: 750 },
  { t: CUT_VOICE, col: ST_DEEPGREEN, dark: true, em: ST_AMBER, x: 300, y: 900 },
  { t: CUT_ANIM, col: ST_BLACK, dark: true, em: '#F08A64', x: 540, y: 750 },
  { t: CUT_TRIO, col: ST_AMBER, dark: false, em: ST_NAVY, x: 540, y: 750 },
  { t: CUT_BRAND, col: ST_NAVY, dark: true, em: '#F08A64', x: 540, y: 750 },
  { t: CUT_LAB, col: null, dark: false, em: null, x: 540, y: 750 },
].map(b => Object.assign(b, { ink: b.dark ? ST_CREAM : C.ink }));
// the flood starts 0.12 s before the cut: half covered ON the cut, done 0.12 s after
const ST_FLOOD = 0.24, ST_LEAD = 0.12;
key code · common_studio.js · the card kit
// the shared kit: a thick-outline card with a hard offset shadow (no blur)
function stBox(K, x, y, w, h, o = {}) {
  const { fill = '#FFFFFF', lw = 5, off = 10, r = 8, line = stLine(), shadow = stShadow() } = o;
  if (off > 0 && shadow) fillRR(K, x + off, y + off, w, h, r, shadow);
  fillRR(K, x, y, w, h, r, fill);
  strokeRR(K, x, y, w, h, r, line, lw);
}
// outline and shadow flip with the background of the frame being drawn
const stLine = () => (stBg(ST_NOW).dark ? ST_CREAM : C.ink);
const stShadow = () => (stBg(ST_NOW).dark ? 'rgba(0,0,0,0.55)' : C.ink);
key code · role_cut.js · 37 → 24 on the words
// /cut: the raw clip is 37 "seconds" of units
// w word · p pause · m mistake · b breath (words sum 24, the rest 13)
const SEGS = [['w', 3], ['p', 1.5], ['w', 2.5], ['b', 1], ['w', 3], ['m', 2], ['p', 2],
  ['w', 3], ['b', 1], ['w', 2.5], ['p', 1.5], ['w', 3], ['m', 1.5], ['w', 2], ['b', 1],
  ['w', 2], ['p', 1.5], ['w', 3]];
const TOTAL = 37, KEEP = 24;
// every mark lands on the word that names it
const T_PAUSE = wi(30), T_MIST = wi(32), T_BREATH = wi(35), T_BECOME = wi(42), T_24 = wi(43);

cue(T_PAUSE, 'tick', -4);
cue(T_MIST, 'stamp', -9);
cue(T_BREATH, 'tick', -4);
cue(T_BECOME + 0.05, 'swoosh', -4);   // the scissors pass, the gaps close
cue(T_24, 'ding', -2);                // counter lands on 24 s and turns green
kick(T_24 + 0.03, 0.8, 0.6);
key code · role_voice.js · /text-behind, depth swap and exploded layers
// /text-behind: the title drops BEHIND the person on "behind",
// then on "part" the three layers fan apart past the card's edges
function shot(K, t) {
  const f = fan(t);
  fillRR(K, VF.x + 12, VF.y + 12, VF.w, VF.h, 14, C.ink);
  if (f <= 0.001) {
    bgLayer(K, t);
    if (behind(t)) { title(K, t, true); personLayer(K, t); }   // title under the cutout
    else { personLayer(K, t); }
  } else {
    layer(K, t, 0, f, () => bgLayer(K, t));                     // background
    layer(K, t, 1, f, () => title(K, t, true));                  // title
    layer(K, t, 2, f, () => personLayer(K, t));                  // you
  }
  // ...frame chrome fades while the layers are apart
  if (!behind(t)) title(K, t, false);   // in front, unclipped: overflows the card
}
LEVEL UP

Two builders at once

The blocks were split between two Claude agents working in parallel: one on the frame, hook, team, brand and CTA (plus the shared kit), the other on the role scenes, which share a small set of drawn helpers (a talking presenter, video frames, sets). It works because both use the same card kit, the same background blocks and the same word clock, so the pieces join without seams.

07 · Decisions

Where the taste is.

01

One deep demo

Fourteen quick demos would be a list. One role shown for real (37 seconds cut to 24) makes the other thirteen believable.

02

Every cue is a word

No animation sits on a guessed second. The pause mark lands on "pause", the counter on "twenty-four", the title drops on "behind".

03

The colour moves first

Each flood starts just before the cut, so the frame is half covered on the cut itself and the new colour never lags behind the voice.

04

Full at the cut

Every block opens with its card already filling the hero zone. A near-empty first frame reads as a glitch on a phone.

05

A corner for the presenter

The bottom-right stays empty in every scene, so Catalina never covers a card and the cards never cover her.

06

Sell the service last

The reel proves the team first and makes the offer only after: your brand, a reel you love, and the keyword.

08 · Watch out

What went wrong, and the fix.

One background reads static

The first pass was mostly cream and felt like one long slide. The fix: a full-frame colour for every block, alternating light and dark.

Colours one block late

The new colour arrived after the cut, so each role started on the previous role's background. The fix: the flood starts 0.12 s before each cut and is half done on the cut.

Near-empty first frames

Some blocks built their card up from nothing, so the first frames after a cut were almost blank. The fix: every block is full at its cut, and the motion happens inside the card.

Small cards

On a phone the role cards were too small to read. The fix: each focus card fills the hero zone of the safe area.

The middle repeated an earlier reel

The first cut demoed the hook, the voice, the animation and 3D, sound and review: the same four steps, with the same props, as one of our earlier reels. The fix: four roles never shown before (subtitles, text behind you, takes, background), each with new props.

A list has no depth

Fourteen roles named one after another felt like a menu. The fix: the /cut block became a real demo, with numbers you can check (37 s in, 24 s out).

09 · Ship it

From render to post.

The render is not the finish line. These steps decide how the reel looks once Instagram compresses it.

Step 01

Export at a real bitrate.

Thick outlines survive compression; thin mono labels and waveforms don't. Encode at 14 Mbps CBR.

Step 02

Check the loudness.

Aim for −14 LUFS with a true peak at or below −1.5 dB, and keep the voice above the sound effects.

Step 03

Make the cover.

The profile grid crops covers to 3:4, so keep the title and the main image between y 240 and 1680 (safer: 300 to 1480).

Step 04

Caption with the credits.

Say what was made and how, give the comment keyword, and credit the voice. On ElevenLabs' free plan, credit it as "Voice: ElevenLabs".

export · ffmpeg
ffmpeg -i render.mp4 -i mix.wav -map 0:v -map 1:a -c:v libx264 -b:v 14M -minrate 14M -maxrate 14M -bufsize 14M -x264-params nal-hrd=cbr -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a aac -b:a 320k -movflags +faststart final.mp4
check loudness · ffmpeg
ffmpeg -i final.mp4 -af ebur128=peak=true -f null -
